question: What are the two distinct phases that make up the process of ejaculation?
explanation: Ejaculation happens in two main sequential steps where fluid gathers in the urethra first and then pushes out. [learn more](GNS121_U4_T5#GNS121_U4_T5_h1)

question: Why is coordination between autonomic and somatic nervous systems necessary for ejaculation?

options.A: It prevents the reabsorption of mature sperm cells
options.B: It maintains a constant blood supply to the skin of the penis
options.C: It regulates the production of testosterone in the testes
options.D: It controls both involuntary gland secretion and voluntary muscle contraction

explanation: Emission relies on autonomic nerve control for fluid release, while expulsion depends on somatic nerves for skeletal muscle action. [learn more](GNS121_U4_T5#GNS121_U4_T5_h1)

question: Which spinal cord segments provide the primary sympathetic innervation responsible for the emission phase?
explanation: The thoracolumbar spinal nerves handle sympathetic signals that trigger smooth muscle contraction during emission. [learn more](GNS121_U4_T5#GNS121_U4_T5_h2)

question: What is the primary function of the pudendal nerve during the ejaculatory process?

options.A: Sending sensory pain signals from the testes to the brain
options.B: Closing the internal urethral sphincter to prevent backflow
options.C: Stimulating the seminal vesicles to produce alkaline fluid
options.D: Directing somatic motor signals to skeletal muscles for expulsion

explanation: The pudendal nerve controls the pelvic floor skeletal muscles that contract rhythmically to push semen out. [learn more](GNS121_U4_T5#GNS121_U4_T5_h2)

question: What primary event defines the completion of the emission phase?

options.A: Semen gathering in the prostatic urethra
options.B: Production of sperm cells in the testes
options.C: Flaccidity of the penile shaft tissue
options.D: Relaxation of the pelvic floor muscles

explanation: Emission finishes when all the fluid components collect in the prostatic urethra right before being pushed out. [learn more](GNS121_U4_T5#GNS121_U4_T5_h3)

question: What is the clinical consequence if the internal urethral sphincter fails to close during emission?
explanation: If the bladder neck does not seal shut, semen takes the path of least resistance and flows backward into the bladder. [learn more](GNS121_U4_T5#GNS121_U4_T5_h3)

question: What type of muscle contractions drive the expulsion phase of ejaculation?
explanation: Pelvic floor skeletal muscles contract in regular bursts to forcefully project the semen out of the body. [learn more](GNS121_U4_T5#GNS121_U4_T5_h4)

question: A patient with pudendal nerve damage will most likely experience a deficit in which part of ejaculation?
explanation: Because the pudendal nerve controls the skeletal muscles responsible for the expulsion phase, damage directly impairs force and flow. [learn more](GNS121_U4_T5#GNS121_U4_T5_h4)

question: What term describes the recovery time after ejaculation when a new erection cannot be achieved?
explanation: The refractory period is the physiological resting phase following orgasm and ejaculation. [learn more](GNS121_U4_T5#GNS121_U4_T5_h5)

question: Which physiological change occurs during the resolution phase of the male sexual response?

options.A: Vasoconstriction reduces blood flow to genital tissues
options.B: Somatic nerve firing rates increase rapidly
options.C: Parasympathetic activity surges to maximum levels
options.D: The internal urethral sphincter opens wide permanently

explanation: Blood vessels constrict to decrease blood flow, allowing the erectile tissues to soften and return to a flaccid state. [learn more](GNS121_U4_T5#GNS121_U4_T5_h5)

question: Which medication class is commonly associated with causing retrograde ejaculation by relaxing the bladder neck?
explanation: Alpha-blockers relax smooth muscle in the prostate and bladder neck, preventing proper closure during emission. [learn more](GNS121_U4_T5#GNS121_U4_T5_h6)

question: Why can retroperitoneal surgery sometimes result in permanent failure of the emission phase?

options.A: It severs the pudendal nerve in the pelvis
options.B: It can damage nearby sympathetic nerve pathways
options.C: It directly destroys the seminal vesicles
options.D: It blocks the urethra with scar tissue

explanation: The sympathetic nerves traveling from T10 to L2 pass through the retroperitoneal space and are vulnerable during extensive surgeries. [learn more](GNS121_U4_T5#GNS121_U4_T5_h6)
